title: ACCY 6100 — Auditing Seminar
subtitle: Modules 5–9 practice quiz
source: Engagement planning, materiality, the audit risk model, ICFR, and evidence (Module 9 slides 1–11 only)

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: On the Module 5 engagement-risk slide, engagement risk is defined as the risk arising from:

choices.text: Sampling error in tests of details
The relationship with a specific client

questions.explanation: Engagement risk is the risk arising from the relationship with a specific client. The slide groups it with the auditor’s business risk, the client’s business risk, and audit risk.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Which of the following is listed on the Module 5 slide as a distinct risk concept alongside engagement risk?
questions.explanation: The slide lists engagement risk, the auditor’s business risk, the client’s business risk, and audit risk.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: According to the planning slide (AS 2101), the engagement partner is responsible for overall quality of the engagement but:

choices.text: May not assign any work to staff
Must also serve as the specialist

questions.explanation: The engagement partner is responsible for overall quality but may delegate responsibilities.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Audit planning involves establishing which pair?

choices.text: The tax provision and the deferred-tax rate
The overall audit strategy and the audit plan
The 10-K cover and the earnings release
The board minutes and the proxy statement

questions.explanation: Planning involves establishing the overall audit strategy and the audit plan.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The slides describe audit planning as:

choices.text: A one-time meeting held only at client acceptance
A task that ends when the engagement letter is signed

questions.explanation: Audit planning is a continual and iterative process, not a single kickoff meeting.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Which of the following is a preliminary engagement activity on the AS 2101 slide?

choices.text: Perform procedures regarding continuance of the audit relationship and determine compliance with independence requirements

questions.explanation: Preliminary activities include procedures regarding continuance of the relationship, independence compliance, and establishing an understanding of the terms with the audit committee.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The auditor should establish an understanding of the terms of the engagement with:
questions.explanation: Establish an understanding of the terms of the engagement with the audit committee.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Judging whether to accept a new client (or retain an existing one) should occur:

choices.text: Only after the audit opinion is drafted
Prior to or with preliminary engagement activities
Only if the prior auditor was sanctioned

questions.explanation: Acceptance/retention should occur prior to or with preliminary engagement activities and be consistent with the firm’s ability to perform the engagement.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Client-acceptance considerations on the slide include whether the firm is independent and whether the services are:

choices.text: Permissible and pre-approved by the audit committee
Guaranteed to produce an unqualified opinion

questions.explanation: Questions include: Is the firm independent? Are the services permissible and pre-approved by the audit committee? Can the auditor access necessary information and have the necessary resources?

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Client acceptance should be based on information about the integrity of the engagement and the integrity of:

choices.text: The client, including management and the audit committee

questions.explanation: Base the decision on information about the integrity of the engagement and the integrity of the client (including management and the audit committee).

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Which of the following is an AS 2101 planning factor the auditor should consider?

choices.text: Knowledge of the company’s ICFR, industry/business matters, recent changes, and preliminary judgments about materiality and risk
Whether the stock is in the Dow Jones Industrial Average

questions.explanation: Planning factors include ICFR knowledge, industry and business matters, recent changes, preliminary materiality and risk judgments, legal/regulatory matters, public information from acceptance/retention, and relative complexity.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The overall audit strategy sets which three elements and then guides the audit plan?

choices.text: Fees, headcount, and the press release date
Scope, timing, and direction of the audit
Tax rate, discount rate, and salvage value
Sample size, confirmation rate, and lockbox location

questions.explanation: Establish an overall audit strategy that sets the scope, timing, and direction of the audit and guides the audit plan.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The audit strategy is affected by the reporting objective of the audit and communication requirements of:
questions.explanation: The strategy is affected by the reporting objective and PCAOB communication requirements, factors important in supervising the team, results of preliminary activities, and the nature, timing, and extent of resources required.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The audit plan (audit program) includes the planned nature, timing, and extent of:

choices.text: Risk assessment procedures, tests of controls and substantive procedures, and other procedures required to comply with PCAOB standards

questions.explanation: The plan includes RAP, tests of controls and substantive procedures, and other planned procedures required to comply with PCAOB standards.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The audit plan should account for procedures performed:

choices.text: Only if the client has no subsidiaries

questions.explanation: The audit plan should account for procedures performed at multiple locations.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: When the plan addresses use of a specialist, the auditor should have sufficient knowledge to communicate the objectives of that person’s work, determine whether the procedures meet the auditor’s objectives, and:

choices.text: Evaluate the results of that person’s procedures
Issue the specialist an audit opinion
Prohibit the specialist from using IT

questions.explanation: The auditor needs enough knowledge to communicate objectives, determine whether the specialist’s procedures meet the auditor’s objectives, and evaluate the results.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The lead auditor is:

choices.text: Any intern who signed the independence confirmation
The firm issuing the report on the client’s financial statements
Always the component auditor of the smallest subsidiary

questions.explanation: Lead auditor = the firm issuing the report on the client’s financial statements.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The engagement team, as defined on the slide, includes accountants and other professional staff employed or engaged by the lead auditor who perform audit procedures, and:

choices.text: Specialists employed by the lead auditor who assist in obtaining or evaluating audit evidence
The referred-to auditor’s entire national office

questions.explanation: Engagement team includes staff who perform procedures or assist the partner, plus specialists employed by the lead auditor who help obtain or evaluate evidence.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: An other auditor is a member of the engagement team who is not:

choices.text: A specialist employed by the client
A partner or employee of the lead auditor, and not working under the lead auditor’s direction as an employee
The engagement quality reviewer employed by the lead auditor

questions.explanation: Other auditor = a member of the engagement team who is not a partner or employee of the lead auditor and is not working under the lead auditor’s direction and functioning as an employee.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: A referred-to auditor is:

choices.text: An audit firm that audits and issues a report on the financial statements of one or more of the client’s business units and is referred to in the lead auditor’s report
A valuation specialist employed by the lead auditor

questions.explanation: Referred-to auditor = a firm that audits a business unit and is referred to in the lead auditor’s report on the client’s financial statements.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: In the PwC / Client A / EY-Germany example, PwC must determine whether it may serve as lead auditor of Client A and use EY’s work on Sub B, and:

choices.text: Whether to fire the audit committee
How using EY’s work will affect the form and content of PwC’s audit report for Client A
Whether EY may set PwC’s materiality
Whether Client A must delist from the NYSE

questions.explanation: PwC must decide whether it can be lead auditor and use EY’s work, and how that use affects the form and content of PwC’s report.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: In determining whether the firm can serve as lead auditor, the engagement partner considers the significance of the portion audited by the firm compared to the financial statements as a whole, the importance of those portions compared with portions audited by other auditors, and:

choices.text: The extent of supervision provided by the engagement partner over work performed by other auditors
Whether the other auditor is cheaper
The number of comment letters from the AICPA

questions.explanation: AS 2101 lead-auditor determination: significance of the portion the firm audited, importance of those portions vs. other auditors’ portions, and extent of EP supervision over other auditors’ work.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The lead auditor should obtain an understanding of the other auditor’s knowledge of SEC and PCAOB independence and ethics requirements, experience applying those requirements, and:

choices.text: The knowledge, skill, and ability of the other auditor’s engagement team members

questions.explanation: Understand the other auditor’s independence/ethics knowledge and experience, and the KSA of that team.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Regarding the other auditor, the lead auditor should obtain representations about policies ensuring SEC/PCAOB compliance, relationships that bear on independence, compliance with those requirements, and whether team members possess the knowledge, skill, and ability to perform assigned tasks. The lead auditor must also determine that it can:

choices.text: Set the other auditor’s partner compensation
Communicate with the other auditor and access the other auditor’s audit documentation
Prohibit the other auditor from using specialists
Issue the other auditor’s local statutory report

questions.explanation: Determine that the lead auditor can communicate with the other auditor and access that auditor’s documentation, and decide whether to refer to the other auditor in the lead auditor’s report.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The engagement partner is the member of the engagement team with primary responsibility for the audit and is responsible for supervising the conduct of the audit and for:
questions.explanation: AS 1201: the EP has primary responsibility, supervises the audit, and is responsible for compliance with audit standards. The EP may delegate supervisory responsibilities.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Supervisors must inform other team members of their responsibilities, including the objectives of the procedures they are to perform, the nature, timing, and extent of those procedures, and:

choices.text: Matters that could impact the procedures or the interpretation of the results

questions.explanation: AS 1201: inform team members of responsibilities, including objectives; nature, timing, and extent; and matters that could affect the procedures or interpretation of results. Direct them to bring significant issues to supervisors, and review their work.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The extent of supervision depends on the nature of the company, the nature of the assigned work, the risk of material misstatement, and:

choices.text: Whether the client is in the S&P 500
The knowledge, skill, and ability of the auditor performing the work
The length of the engagement letter

questions.explanation: AS 1201: extent of supervision depends on the company, the assigned work, RMM, and the KSA of the auditor doing the work.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: AS 1301 communications at appointment or retention and regarding audit planning include obtaining information relevant to the audit by asking the audit committee about their knowledge of relevant matters, and communicating:

choices.text: Overall audit strategy, timing, and risks

questions.explanation: Planning communications: obtain information from the AC, and communicate overall strategy, timing, and risks.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Planning communications with the audit committee also cover the nature and extent of specialized skill or knowledge needed, use of internal audit, use of personnel under the direction of management, involvement of other auditors, and:

choices.text: The basis for the auditor’s determination that it can serve as lead auditor

questions.explanation: The slide lists specialized skill/knowledge needed, internal audit use, company personnel under management’s direction, other auditors involved, and the basis for serving as lead auditor.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Detailed communications regarding the results of the audit are in AS 1301; the Module 5 slide says those communications:

choices.text: Are optional if the opinion is unqualified
Will be discussed in later modules
Are made only to the PCAOB

questions.explanation: The slide points to AS 1301 for results communications and notes they will be discussed later.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between the audit strategy and the audit plan on these slides?

choices.text: They are identical documents with two names
The strategy sets scope, timing, and direction; the plan specifies the nature, timing, and extent of procedures
The strategy is for tax; the plan is for ICFR only
The plan is written by the audit committee

questions.explanation: Strategy = scope, timing, direction (and guides the plan). Plan/program = planned NTE of RAP, tests of controls, substantive procedures, and other PCAOB-required procedures.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Client acceptance must be consistent with:

choices.text: The client’s desired earnings per share
The firm’s ability to perform the engagement
The lowest bid on the RFP
Whether the prior auditor was a Big Four firm

questions.explanation: Acceptance/retention should be consistent with the firm’s ability to perform the engagement (independence, permissible services, access, resources).

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Public information about the company and knowledge gained during client acceptance and retention is listed as a factor in:

choices.text: Selecting the company’s auditor of record at the SEC

questions.explanation: AS 2101 planning factors include public information and knowledge from acceptance/retention.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: The lead auditor must determine whether to refer to the other auditor in:
questions.explanation: Determine whether to refer to the other auditor in the lead auditor’s report.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Directing team members to bring significant issues to the attention of supervisors is a responsibility of:

choices.text: Supervisors (the engagement partner and those to whom supervisory responsibilities have been delegated)
The PCAOB only after an inspection

questions.explanation: AS 1201 supervisors inform the team of responsibilities, direct them to escalate significant issues, and review their work.

questions.module: Module 5: Audit Planning — The Engagement
questions.prompt: Which standard is the Module 5 home for supervision of the audit engagement?
questions.explanation: Supervision is AS 1201. Planning is AS 2101. Audit-committee communications are AS 1301.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: The opening materiality slide asks, for planning: “How much misstatement are you willing not to know about?” That question is paired with effort, which asks:

choices.text: How large is the audit committee?
How much audit evidence is enough?
How many comment letters did the SEC send?
How high is the stock price?

questions.explanation: Planning ↔ how much misstatement you are willing not to know about. Effort ↔ how much evidence is enough. Results evaluation, interpretation/value, and quality/legal-liability questions sit alongside. Audit risk and materiality are central to auditing.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: The concept of materiality recognizes that some matters, facts, or misstatements of facts, individually or in the aggregate:

choices.text: Must always be booked if they exceed $1
Are important to decision makers while others are not
Are relevant only to the tax provision

questions.explanation: Some matters, individually or in the aggregate, are important to decision makers; others are not.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: The U.S. Supreme Court formulation quoted on the slide (and in AS 2105) is that a fact is material if there is a substantial likelihood that the reasonable investor would have viewed it as having significantly altered:

choices.text: The “total mix” of information made available

questions.explanation: Substantial likelihood the fact would have been viewed by the reasonable investor as significantly altering the total mix of information made available. Determinations require delicate assessments of the inferences a reasonable shareholder would draw.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: FASB Concepts Statement No. 8, as quoted, says an omission or misstatement is material if, in light of surrounding circumstances, the magnitude is such that it is probable that the judgment of a reasonable person would have been:

choices.text: Unaffected if disclosed in a footnote only
Changed by the inclusion or correction of the item
Relevant solely to creditors, never investors
Immaterial whenever it is less than 10% of assets

questions.explanation: Probable that the judgment of a reasonable person would have been changed by including or correcting the item.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Because of the nature of audit evidence and the characteristics of fraud, the auditor is able to obtain (AS 1001):

choices.text: Absolute assurance that all fraud is detected
Reasonable, but not absolute, assurance that material misstatements are detected

questions.explanation: Reasonable, not absolute, assurance that material misstatements are detected.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Audit risk is the risk that the auditor may unknowingly fail to appropriately modify his or her opinion on financial statements that are:
questions.explanation: Audit risk is defined in terms of material misstatement. Therefore the auditor must determine materiality before she can assess risk.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: A key takeaway on the materiality/audit-risk slide is that audit risk is defined in terms of materiality; therefore the auditor must determine materiality:

choices.text: Only after the opinion is signed
Using the Supreme Court’s numerical threshold of 5%

questions.explanation: Determine materiality first; then assess risk. The Supreme Court test is qualitative (“total mix”), not a bright-line percentage.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Materiality is based on the auditor’s assessment of the needs of users. Which users?

choices.text: Each individual known shareholder, whose needs are modeled separately
Users as a group; the auditor does not consider the needs of individual users because those needs vary widely

questions.explanation: Do not consider individual users’ needs. Those needs vary widely.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: According to ISA 320 as presented, reasonable shareholders have a reasonable knowledge of business and economic activities and accounting and a willingness to study the financial statements with:

choices.text: No effort, because audits replace reading

questions.explanation: Reasonable knowledge plus willingness to study the information with reasonable diligence.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: ISA 320’s reasonable shareholders understand that materiality is applied when financial statements are prepared, presented, and audited; recognize that uncertainties are inherent in estimates, judgment, and beliefs about future events; and:

choices.text: Never make decisions from the statements
Make economic decisions based on the financial statements

questions.explanation: They make economic decisions based on the financial statements.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: For planning purposes, materiality is determined first for:

choices.text: The financial statements taken as a whole, expressed as a specific amount

questions.explanation: First assess materiality for the FS as a whole, as a specific amount. That amount is not a threshold below which misstatements are automatically immaterial.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Planning materiality for the financial statements as a whole is:

choices.text: A threshold below which all misstatements are considered immaterial
Not a threshold below which misstatements are considered immaterial
Set by the audit committee, not the auditor

questions.explanation: The slide is explicit: this level is not a threshold below which misstatements are considered immaterial. (Hence the “Is $1 million material?” discussion prompt.)

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Materiality is determined in a quantitative and qualitative manner and will generally be:

choices.text: A round number unrelated to the financial statements
A percentage of a chosen benchmark
The same dollar amount for every public company

questions.explanation: Quantitative and qualitative. Generally a % of a benchmark. As the chosen benchmark grows, so does the assessment of materiality.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: The auditor chooses a financial statement benchmark against which to assess materiality by considering the needs of users — specifically, which parts of the financial statements:

choices.text: Impact user decisions or judgments the most

questions.explanation: Choose the benchmark by considering users: what parts of the FS impact their decisions most?

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: For most profit-oriented companies, the slides say to base materiality on a measure of:
questions.explanation: For most profit-oriented companies, base materiality on a measure of profit/earnings, because that is what users typically focus on.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Why not always base materiality on earnings?

choices.text: Because PCAOB rules forbid earnings-based materiality
Earnings may not be useful (volatile, losses, etc.), or users may focus on other FS components
Because only assets are allowed as a base

questions.explanation: Use other bases when earnings are volatile, the company suffers losses, or investors focus on other components.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: ISA 320 factors that may affect identification of an appropriate benchmark include the elements of the financial statements, items on which users’ attention tends to be focused, the nature of the entity and where it is in its life cycle, the industry and economic environment, ownership and financing, and:

choices.text: The relative volatility of the benchmark

questions.explanation: Plus: choosing the right basis is a matter of auditor judgment.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: The first level of materiality is materiality for the financial statements as a whole: the maximum amount of misstatement that can exist and the FS still be considered fairly stated, determined by applying an appropriate % to the chosen basis. A problem for the auditor is that she is not likely to:

choices.text: Find all misstatements that actually exist

questions.explanation: She is not likely to find all misstatements that actually exist — which is why tolerable misstatement and an accumulation threshold sit below overall materiality.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Tolerable misstatement is:

choices.text: The same as a material weakness
The maximum amount of misstatement in a specific balance or class of transactions the auditor is willing to accept, allowing for the aggregate of uncorrected and undetected misstatements
The amount users will never notice, by statute

questions.explanation: Second level: tolerable misstatement at the balance/class level, allowing for uncorrected + undetected misstatements in the aggregate.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Under ASB and IAASB standards, “performance materiality” is equivalent to the PCAOB’s notion of:
questions.explanation: ASB 320 / ISA 320 “performance materiality” ≈ PCAOB “tolerable” misstatement. Under ASB/IAASB, “tolerable misstatement” is also used when planning specific procedures (e.g., sample size for a test of details).

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: The third level is the threshold for accumulating misstatements: a threshold below which a misstatement would be:

choices.text: Clearly trivial; such misstatements are ignored for later individual and aggregate evaluation
Reported to the SEC within four days

questions.explanation: Below the accumulation/clearly-trivial threshold, misstatements are ignored. Above it, they are evaluated individually and aggregated.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Overall FS materiality could be set at lower levels for certain accounts and disclosures when:

choices.text: The partner wants a round number
Circumstances indicate that user decisions could be affected by smaller amounts of misstatement
The client requests a smaller number
The prior year was a review, not an audit

questions.explanation: Rules of thumb on the slide include lowering materiality for particular accounts/disclosures when users could be affected by smaller misstatements.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: In order, the three levels of materiality assessments on the slides are:

choices.text: FS as a whole; tolerable misstatement; threshold for accumulating (clearly trivial) misstatements

questions.explanation: 1st overall FS materiality, 2nd tolerable misstatement, 3rd accumulating/clearly trivial threshold.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: “Delicate assessments of the inferences a reasonable shareholder would draw” is language from:

choices.text: The U.S. Supreme Court, as quoted in connection with AS 2105

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court language is on the materiality slides and is tied to AS 2105.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Which statement about the $1 million discussion prompt is most faithful to the slides?

choices.text: $1 million is always material for every issuer
Whether $1 million is material depends on surrounding circumstances and users; a raw dollar amount is not enough
$1 million is the PCAOB’s bright-line rule
$1 million is clearly trivial for all public companies

questions.explanation: The slide asks “Is $1 million material? Why or why not?” precisely because overall planning materiality is a specific amount but is not a mechanical immateriality threshold, and qualitative context matters.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: As the chosen benchmark grows, the assessment of materiality:

choices.text: Must switch from earnings to assets

questions.explanation: As the chosen benchmark grows, so does the assessment of materiality.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Results evaluation on the opening slide asks:

choices.text: How much misstatement can you waive and still meet GAAP?
Whether COSO is a recognized framework

questions.explanation: The five framing questions: planning (willing not to know), effort (enough evidence), results evaluation (waive and still meet GAAP), interpretation/value (how much users discount audited information), quality/legal (enough auditing to avoid legal liability).

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Quality evaluation on that same slide is framed as:

choices.text: Have you done enough auditing to avoid legal liability?

questions.explanation: Quality evaluation ↔ enough auditing to avoid legal liability.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Interpretation (or value) asks how much audited (GAAP-based) information is:
questions.explanation: How much is audited GAAP information discounted by the user/decision maker?

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Choosing the right basis for determining materiality is based on:

choices.text: A statutory table in the Securities Act
The prior auditor’s exact dollar amount, reused forever

questions.explanation: The slide closes: choosing the right basis is based on auditor judgment, informed by ISA 320-type factors.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Under ASB/IAASB terminology as contrasted on the slide, “tolerable misstatement” is a level of materiality used to:

choices.text: Plan specific auditing procedures (e.g., determining a sample size for a test of details)

questions.explanation: Careful with vocabulary: PCAOB “tolerable” ≈ ASB/IAASB “performance materiality.” ASB/IAASB “tolerable” is used in planning specific procedures such as TOD sample size.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Misstatements below the accumulating threshold:

choices.text: Must be communicated as a material weakness

questions.explanation: Clearly trivial misstatements are ignored. Above the threshold, evaluate individually and in the aggregate.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: The auditor applies an appropriate percentage to the chosen basis to compute:

choices.text: Materiality for the financial statements as a whole

questions.explanation: Overall FS materiality = appropriate % × chosen basis = maximum misstatement that can exist with the FS still fairly stated.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the course’s logic connecting materiality to risk?

choices.text: Assess ARM first, then ignore materiality
Determine materiality, because audit risk is defined in terms of material misstatement, then assess risk
Set DR first, then pick a benchmark at random
Wait until the opinion date to think about users

questions.explanation: AR is the risk of failing to modify the opinion on materially misstated FS. Materiality comes first.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: FASB CON 8’s “probable that the judgment of a reasonable person would have been changed” is presented as:

choices.text: A conceptual definition of materiality, alongside the Supreme Court’s “total mix” language

questions.explanation: Two definitions sit on the concept slide: FASB CON 8 (magnitude / reasonable person) and the Supreme Court (total mix / reasonable investor). The slide even asks what might be missing from those explanations.

questions.module: Module 6: Audit Planning — Materiality
questions.prompt: The Supreme Court notes that determinations of materiality require delicate assessments of inferences a reasonable shareholder would draw from a given set of facts and:

choices.text: The significance of those inferences to him
Whether the misstatement is in an unaudited exhibit

questions.explanation: Quoted on multiple Module 6 slides: inferences a reasonable shareholder would draw, and the significance of those inferences to him.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: A risk-based audit approach is designed to efficiently and effectively focus the nature, timing, and extent of procedures on areas with the most potential for causing:

choices.text: Material misstatement(s) in the financial report

questions.explanation: Figure out where material misstatements are most likely and focus resources there to achieve a certain level of audit risk. Apply the ARM.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: On the slides, Audit Risk = 1 − Assurance, and Acceptable Audit Risk = 1 − Reasonable assurance. Audit Risk also equals:

choices.text: Risk of Material Misstatement × Detection Risk

questions.explanation: AR = RMM × DR, and RMM = IR × CR, so AR = IR × CR × DR.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: The algebraic audit risk model on the slides is:
questions.explanation: AR = IR × CR × DR. Planned DR is the residual: Planned DR = AR / (IR × CR).

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Who chooses (sets) the level of inherent risk?

choices.text: The auditor, by picking sample size
Management chooses lines of business and transactions that impact IR; other factors may be out of management’s control. The auditor only assesses IR and does not control/choose it
The PCAOB, in every inspection report
The audit committee, by setting materiality

questions.explanation: IR is the likelihood of a material misstatement without considering internal controls. Auditor assesses; does not choose.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Inherent risk is:

choices.text: The risk the auditor’s procedures fail
The likelihood of a material misstatement without considering the effects of internal controls
The risk controls fail to operate

questions.explanation: IR ignores controls by definition.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Control risk is the likelihood that a material misstatement that would otherwise occur will not be:

choices.text: Detected, prevented, or corrected by the internal control system

questions.explanation: CR is about the IC system’s failure to prevent/detect/correct.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Who chooses the level of control risk?

choices.text: The auditor, by calculating planned DR
Management chooses the quality of the IC system (investment in ICFR and the control environment). The auditor only assesses CR and does not control/choose it

questions.explanation: Management chooses IC quality; the auditor assesses CR.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Detection risk is the likelihood that the audit will not detect material misstatements that occur and:

choices.text: Are still in the unaudited trial balance before any work
Are not detected, prevented, or corrected by the internal control system

questions.explanation: DR is residual after IR and CR: misstatements that occur and get through controls, then also get through the audit.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Who chooses the level of detection risk?

choices.text: The auditor uses the ARM to calculate a planned level of detection risk

questions.explanation: Planned DR = Audit Risk / (IR × CR). That planned DR drives how persuasive substantive evidence needs to be (nature, timing, and extent).

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: The formula on the detection-risk slide is Planned Detection Risk =
questions.explanation: Planned DR = AR / (IR × CR) = AR / RMM.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: The calculated planned DR is used to determine:

choices.text: How persuasive the substantive evidence needs to be — the nature, timing, and extent of substantive procedures

questions.explanation: Planned DR → persuasiveness of substantive evidence (NTE).

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Achieved DR (and consequently achieved audit risk) depends on:

choices.text: The procedures actually chosen and the quality of their implementation
Whether COSO or Turnbull is used

questions.explanation: Planned DR is a target. Achieved DR depends on what you actually did and how well you did it.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: When planned DR is higher, the auditor is willing to accept a higher probability of missing a misstatement that got through controls, and therefore can accept evidence that is:

choices.text: Obtained only after the report date

questions.explanation: Higher planned DR → less persuasive evidence is acceptable.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: When planned DR is lower, the auditor must obtain evidence that is:
questions.explanation: Lower planned DR → more persuasive evidence.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Each ARM component is defined in terms of materiality. Holding all else equal, increasing materiality decreases RMM, which:

choices.text: Decreases planned DR and requires more persuasive evidence
Increases planned DR and allows less persuasive evidence

questions.explanation: Increasing materiality >>> decreasing RMM >>> increasing Planned DR >>> less persuasive evidence. Decreasing materiality does the opposite.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Decreasing materiality, holding all else equal, leads to:

choices.text: Increasing RMM, decreasing planned DR, more persuasive evidence

questions.explanation: Decreasing materiality >>> increasing RMM >>> decreasing Planned DR >>> more persuasive evidence.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: Joe will buy a bag of 1,000 pearls if no more than 30 are defective. With AuR = 5% and IR × CR = 100%, planned DR equals:
questions.explanation: Planned DR = AuR / (IR × CR) = 5% / 100% = 5%. N = 1000; “materiality” is 30 defectives.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: To drive achieved DR down to about 4.9% (near the 5% planned DR) when materiality is 30 defectives in 1,000, Joe needs about how many pearls?
questions.explanation: 99 pearls: achieved DR ≈ 4.9%.

questions.prompt: If materiality increases to 60 defectives in 1,000, drawing 1 pearl gives achieved DR of:

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: With materiality of 60 defectives, about how many pearls get achieved DR to ~4.8%?
questions.explanation: 50 pearls ≈ 4.8%. Increasing materiality reduces required sample size.

questions.module: Module 7: The Audit Risk Model and Inherent Risk
questions.prompt: If materiality decreases to 15 defectives, 1 pearl gives achieved DR of 98.5%, and getting to ~4.9% takes about:

questions.prompt: In the pearl example, when RMM = 1, planned DR = .05 and n = 99. When RMM = .5, planned DR = .10 and n =
